<p></p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) observatory marks not only the first hardware collaboration on an Earth mission between NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), but also the first satellite to bring together L-band and S-band radar on one spacecraft. The combination makes for an exceptionally powerful synthetic aperture radar that will provide high-resolution data enabling scientists to comprehensively monitor the planet’s land and ice surfaces like never before, building a detailed record of how they change over time.</p>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Here’s a closer look at the spacecraft:</p>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<ul class="wp-block-list"></p>
<li><strong>2:</strong> Number of science instruments — an L-band synthetic aperture radar system and an S-band synthetic aperture radar system</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>18</strong> <strong>feet</strong> (5.5 meters): Length of spacecraft body and radar instrument payload</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>18</strong> <strong>feet</strong> (5.5 meters): Length of each of the spacecraft’s two deployable motorized solar arrays, totaling about 250 square feet (23 square meters) in area. Together, they provide about 5 kilowatts of power.</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>39 feet </strong>(12 meters): Diameter of the radar antenna reflector, which resembles a snare drum. The reflector will deploy on a boom that is about 30 feet (9 meters) long.</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>15:</strong> Number of thrusters</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>5,250 pounds</strong> (2,380 kilograms): Approximate mass of the satellite, including propellant, at the time of launch</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>90 days:</strong> How long the commissioning phase is expected to last after launch. During this period, the mission team will check out spacecraft systems, deploy the boom and giant radar antenna reflector, and assess the performance of the radar instruments. Science operations begin after completion of the commissioning phase.</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>14:</strong> Number of times a day NISAR will circle Earth, orbiting at an altitude of 464 miles (747 kilometers). In doing so, NISAR will scan nearly all the planet’s land and ice surfaces twice every 12 days.</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>80 terabytes:</strong> How much data NISAR will send to Earth daily — enough data to fill about 150 512-gigabyte hard drives each day</li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>0.4 inches</strong> (1 centimeter): How much vertical movement NISAR can detect over a plot of land or ice surface about the size of half a tennis court </li>
<p></p>
<p></p>
<li><strong>3 years:</strong> Duration of NISAR’s prime mission</li>
<p></ul>
<p></p>
<p></p>

NASA comes to Instagram with stunning moon pictures

NASA has joined the world of Instagram - and has already attracted an incredible 56,374 followers within hours of posting its first pictures on the social media site.
PTI
Updated: Sep 8, 2013, 01:04PM IST
Prefer us on
WASHINGTON: NASA has joined the world of Instagram - and has already attracted an incredible 56,374 followers within hours of posting its first pictures on the social media site.
The US space agency posted two images for its debut. One of the images was a detailed picture of the moon and its grey, pock-marked surface.
The second one was a stunning Earth-rise. NASA promised many more photos would be posted soon.
"We're constantly looking to expand our social media portfolio to include tools that will best tell NASA's story of exploration and discovery," said NASA Press Secretary Lauren Worley.
"Instagram has a passionate following of users who are hungry for new and exciting photos. We believe we have some of the most engaging images on and off the planet - and we can't wait to engage with Instagrammers," said Worley.
"Aeronautics, astrophysics, Earth science, human spaceflight and more, the NASA account will provide a comprehensive view of the agency by sharing new and historic images and videos," the space agency said on its website.
The first NASA posts also highlight the launch of the agency's Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer (LADEE), from its Wallops Flight Facility on Wallops Island, Virginia.
LADEE is a robotic research mission that will orbit the moon to gather detailed information about the structure and composition of the thin lunar atmosphere and determine whether dust is being lofted into the lunar sky.

Given their numbers, chances are decent that you already follow them in some way — be it on Instagram, Twitter, or Facebook — but let us assure you they have other accounts and cooler accounts Every single NASA center and facility has its own set of social media pages. So different organizations and programs run directly under NASA, or are they affiliated with the agency in some way, as do the different ongoing major missions and research topics. And let’s not forget the several dozen NASA astronauts and experts that have their own feeds to share. </p><p>Altogether, NASA lists 200 different people, organizations, or institutions that run at least one or more social media pages. We dug through them all to find out which NASA accounts possessed the coolest — and strangest — social media feeds. Here they are!</p><h4>NASA Instagram (<a href="https://www.instagram.com/nasa/" target="_blank">@NASA</a>)</h4><p>Easily the best social media page NASA runs. Though not as popular as NASA’s <a href="https://www.facebook.com/NASA/" target="_blank">Facebook</a> and <a href="https://twitter.com/nasa" target="_blank">Twitter</a> pages in terms of sheer numbers, the Instagram page is your go-to for all your space porn needs. </p><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:658px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="BCT MJ1"><div class="A7C" style="padding-top:74.60317460317461%;"></div><blockquote class="UyF" data-instgrm-permalink="https://www.instagram.com/p/BAsUuuIoaEI" data-shortcode="BAsUuuIoaEI"><div class="yzx"><a target="_blank" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/BAsUuuIoaEI" class="y9v GmH" title="View on Instagram"><i class="icx g9F"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><p>It’s important to note this Instagram page often pulls from other NASA-affiliated accounts and reposts the best or most compelling images. So if you’re following a ton of different space-related Instagram feeds, chances are you’ll run into quite a few repeats. Still, this is by far one of the best Instagram pages you have the opportunity to follow.</p><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:658px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="BCT MJ1"><div class="A7C" style="padding-top:74.60317460317461%;"></div><blockquote class="UyF" data-instgrm-permalink="https://www.instagram.com/p/BAf0hW0IaBD" data-shortcode="BAf0hW0IaBD"><div class="yzx"><a target="_blank" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/BAf0hW0IaBD" class="y9v GmH" title="View on Instagram"><i class="icx g9F"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA Vine (<a href="https://vine.co/nasa" target="_blank">@NASA</a>)</h4><p>Well, it didn’t take long to finally find a weird NASA social media page. NASA’s Vine feed doesn’t have the mainstream allure of its Instagram. No, the Vine page is just plain full of hypnotizing loops — some beautiful, some bizarre. Nearly all of them are ‘revines’ from other accounts, but this is still probably the best aggregate mix of space-related vines that let you embrace space as a series of flat-circle snippets. </p><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:600px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="KTw"><div class="tu9" data-iframe-src="https://vine.co/v/eLTFBDD0KMW/embed/simple"></div></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:600px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="KTw"><div class="tu9" data-iframe-src="https://vine.co/v/exL9lEvKqrE/embed/simple"></div></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:600px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="KTw"><div class="tu9" data-iframe-src="https://vine.co/v/eBIOgpZYb2K/embed/simple"></div></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA <a href="https://soundcloud.com/nasa" target="_blank">Soundcloud</a></h4><p>If images and videos aren’t enough, NASA has a Soundcloud page that’s chock-full of all — and I mean <em>all</em> — the various kinds of space-related sounds you’ve been dying to listen to. From rocket engine sounds, to radio waves collected by different probes, and even what was sent up on the old <a href="https://www.inverse.com/article/4950-nasa-s-record-for-extraterrestials-is-easy-listening">Golden Record</a> onboard the Voyager spacecraft back in 1977. </p><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:500px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="L3D"><div class="tu9" data-iframe-src="https://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https://soundcloud.com/nasa/voyager-lightning-on-jupiter"></div></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:500px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="L3D"><div class="tu9" data-iframe-src="https://w.soundcloud.com/player/?url=https://soundcloud.com/nasa/atlas-v-launch"></div></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA Jet Propulsion Lab <a href="https://www.youtube.com/user/JPLnews" target="_blank">YouTube Channel</a></h4><p>NASA JPL is responsible for some of the most amazing research and development done at the space agency — from creating and testing robotic spacecraft (like the <em>Curiosity</em> rover), to overseeing the NuSTAR x-ray telescope mission. Not so surprisingly, JPL boasts a fascinating and incredibly educational YouTube channel that offers a slew of different videos keeping NASA fans up to date on what’s going on, as well as some really great mini-documentaries that explore some of the most captivating questions the agency as a whole is trying to investigate right now.</p><div class="sWr iGR" style="max-width:854px;"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="bwd"><noscript><iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/1tUSiWLyN9A" data-videoid="1tUSiWLyN9A" class="TVx"></iframe></noscript></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA360 Twitter (<a href="https://twitter.com/NASA360" target="_blank">@NASA360</a>)</h4><p>I’ll just let the account description sell itself: </p><blockquote class="tDr">“Artfully charming, award-winning, hipster-friendly NASA authority. Prone to fits of awesomeness. Friends of organisms everywhere. We make a TV show too!”</blockquote><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="687314138196910081"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/nasa360/status/687314138196910081" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="688432713892794368"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/nasa360/status/688432713892794368" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="688077760003084288"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/nasa360/status/688077760003084288" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA History <a href="https://www.facebook.com/NASAHistoryOffice" target="_blank">Facebook</a></h4><p>Although space exploration focuses on the future, there’s plenty of amazing things to learn about NASA and its 60+ year history. The Facebook page is filled with a ton of amazing posts going over milestones and hidden factoids alike. It’s basically a #tbt every day at NASA History.</p><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="_-W" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/NASAHistoryOffice/posts/1061925527192462:0" data-width="auto" data-show-text="true"></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="_-W" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/NASAHistoryOffice/posts/1059367717448243:0" data-width="auto" data-show-text="true"></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>NASA Space Biology <a href="https://www.facebook.com/spacebiology/timeline" target="_blank">Facebook</a></h4><p>You want to talk about life in space? Go to this page, run by NASA Ames Research Center. ‘Nuff said.</p><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="_-W" data-href="https://www.facebook.com/NASA/posts/10153735189401772:0" data-width="auto" data-show-text="true"></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>Women@NASA Twitter (<a href="https://twitter.com/WomenNASA" target="_blank">@WomenNASA</a>)</h4><p>Perhaps the most important social media page on this list, Women@NASA is the official agency program dedicated to inspiring girls and young women to get involved with STEM research. Space exploration has been dominated by men since its inception. That’s changing, and programs like this are part of the reason.</p><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="666261981750513664"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/womennasa/status/666261981750513664" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="685107952269803520"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/womennasa/status/685107952269803520" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>Asteroid Watch Twitter (<a href="https://twitter.com/asteroidwatch" target="_blank">@AsteroidWatch</a>)</h4><p>If you’re obsessed with comets, asteroids, and other balls of ice and rock zooming around the solar system, you’ll want to keep close tabs on this Twitter feed. If there’s a big rock on its way to hit the earth and annihilate us all, Asteroid Watch will be the first to let you know.  </p><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="685182401736081409"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/asteroidwatch/status/685182401736081409" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><div class="sWr iGR"><div class><figure class="VE7"><div><div class="XUu RK-"><blockquote data-tweetid="652213754944294912"><div class="Jen"><a target="_blank" href="https://twitter.com/asteroidwatch/status/652213754944294912" class="y9v W3A" title="View on X"><i class="icx b18"></i></a></div></blockquote></div></div></figure></div></div><h4>Astronaut Scott Kelly’s Instagram (<a href="https://www.instagram.com/stationcdrkelly/" target="_blank">@stationcdrkelly</a>)</h4><p>There are obviously too many astronauts and NASA scientists to follow, but the one you <em>need</em> to follow is Scott Kelly — currently hanging out at the International Space Station right now on his “Year in Space” mission to study the effects of long-term zero-gravity habitation on the human body.
